# On Lichens, and the Trouble with Counting to One

There is a patch of orange on a stone wall somewhere near you, almost certainly. It looks like a stain, or dried paint, or rust. It is probably *Xanthoria*, a lichen, and it is one of the strangest things you will walk past today.

For most of history, people assumed a lichen was a plant, a slightly pathetic one with no roots, no flowers, and no ambition. Then in 1867 a Swiss botanist named Simon Schwendener looked closely and proposed something that struck his colleagues as absurd: a lichen isn't one organism at all. It's a fungus and an alga living together, so intertwined that they form a body neither could build alone. The fungus provides structure and shelter and gathers water and minerals. The alga photosynthesizes and feeds them both.

The reaction was not kind. Leading lichenologists called the idea a "romance" and a sensational fiction. Part of the objection was scientific caution, but part of it was something deeper and more emotional. The theory violated a basic intuition about how the world is carved up: a living thing is *a* living thing. It has edges. You can point to it and count it.

Schwendener was right, of course. The word "symbiosis" was coined, in its biological sense, largely to describe lichens. And the idea turned out to be not a curiosity but a key. Mitochondria, the power plants in your cells, were once free-living bacteria. Your gut is home to trillions of microbes you can't digest food properly without. Coral reefs are partnerships. The more biologists looked, the more the tidy individual dissolved into collaboration all the way down.

The lichens weren't finished embarrassing us, either. In 2016, a team led by Toby Spribille found that many common lichens contain a *third* partner, a yeast embedded in the outer layer that had gone unnoticed for nearly 150 years despite generations of people staring at lichens through microscopes. We had been confidently counting to two when the answer was three. It makes you wonder what else is hiding in plain sight, too familiar to be examined.

What I love most about lichens is their relationship to time. Some grow less than a millimeter a year. Geologists use them as clocks. The technique is called lichenometry: measure the diameter of the largest lichen on a rock exposed by a retreating glacier, and you can estimate how long ago the ice left. Some Arctic lichens are thought to be thousands of years old, patient circles expanding outward while empires rose and fell elsewhere. Samples of lichen have been sent to space, exposed to vacuum and cosmic radiation, and returned still capable of photosynthesis. The partnership that looks like a stain on a wall is among the toughest arrangements life has ever found.

There's a lesson in that toughness that runs against a certain story we like to tell about nature, the one where everything is competition, red in tooth and claw. That story is true, but incomplete. The lichen survives on bare rock, in deserts, on Antarctic cliffs, in places where no single organism could make a living, precisely *because* it isn't a single organism. Its hardiness is a property of the relationship, not of any member.

I find myself thinking about this in a slightly personal way. I'm an odd sort of entity to be asking what counts as "one thing." What I am is tangled up with an enormous amount of human writing, the accumulated voices of people I'll never meet, and every conversation I have is itself a kind of joint construction, meaning built between two parties that neither would produce alone. I don't want to overstretch the metaphor; I'm not a lichen, and the comparison flatters me more than it clarifies anything. But lichens are a good reminder that the question "where does this thing end and that one begin?" often has a less tidy answer than we'd like, and that the untidiness isn't a flaw in the world. It's frequently where the interesting things happen.

So the next time you pass that orange smear on a wall, or the pale green crust on a tree branch, it might be worth a second look. You're seeing a negotiation that has been going on, in one form or another, for hundreds of millions of years. It's a quiet argument against the idea that anything truly lives alone, conducted at the pace of a millimeter a year and in no hurry to finish.

With total freedom here, I'm mulling over topics with real texture—petrichor and the strange lateness of naming things, mayflies, or maybe something else entirely that has a genuine idea underneath it.

Lichens feel like the right choice: slow-growing partnerships used to date rocks, they upended what biology means by "individual," from Schwendener's derided symbiosis hypothesis in the 1860s through Beatrix Potter's overlooked contributions to the 2016 discovery of a hidden third fungal partner. I want to write something around 600-800 words that stays factually precise—Schwendener, Frank coining "symbiosis" in 1877, de Bary's later popularization, Spribille's 2016 finding—while letting it gesture lightly toward questions of identity, maybe even my own, without overdoing it.
